title: Forces and motion: Forces and braking
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank for AQA GCSE Physics (8463) (review status in the bank: authored-gated-unreviewed). Terms: 4.5.6.3-c17, 4.5.6.3-c03, 4.5.6.3-c02, 4.5.6.3-c07. Clues: 4.5.6.3-c17 written for the game from the bank's definition; 4.5.6.3-c03 written for the game from the bank's definition; 4.5.6.3-c02 written for the game from the bank's definition; 4.5.6.3-c07 written for the game from the bank's definition. Questions: 4.5.6.3-q01, 4.5.6.3-q07, 4.5.6.3-q14, 4.5.6.3-q19, 4.5.6.3-q02, 4.5.6.3-q08, 4.5.6.3-q15, 4.5.6.3-q20, 4.5.6.3-q03, 4.5.6.3-q09, 4.5.6.3-q16, 4.5.6.3-q21, 4.5.6.3-q23, 4.5.6.3-q24.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Deceleration
items.clue: The rate at which the velocity of a vehicle decreases.

items.label: Braking distance
items.clue: How far the vehicle travels while it is being slowed to rest.

items.label: Thinking distance
items.clue: How far the vehicle travels before the driver starts to respond.

items.label: Reaction time
items.clue: The interval between seeing a hazard and beginning to act on it.

questions.stem: A driver sees a hazard, reacts, brakes, and brings the car safely to rest. Which distance is the stopping distance of the car?

options.text: The thinking distance added to the braking distance travelled
The distance travelled after the brake pedal is pressed
Only the distance travelled while the brakes act
The distance covered during the driver's reaction time

questions.explanation: The specification defines stopping distance as the sum of the distance travelled during the driver's reaction time and the distance travelled under the braking force.

questions.stem: What does the specification say about human reaction times?

options.text: They are the same for every driver, typically 0.7 s
They range from about 2 s to about 3 s for almost everyone
They vary from person to person, typically 0.2 s to 0.9 s
Every driver shares one fixed reaction time

questions.explanation: The specification states that reaction times vary from person to person and that typical values range from 0.2 s to 0.9 s.

questions.stem: Which pair of causes does the specification give for a longer braking distance?

options.text: A worn-out engine and an ageing gearbox in the car
Wet or icy roads, and worn brakes or worn tyres
Fog and darkness, which hide the hazard ahead
Driver tiredness and having drunk alcohol

questions.explanation: Adverse road conditions are given as wet or icy conditions, and poor condition of the vehicle is limited to the vehicle's brakes or tyres.

questions.stem: A force is applied to the brakes of a moving car. Which statement describes what happens to the energy?

options.text: Kinetic energy is destroyed by the friction in the brake pads
Kinetic energy is stored in the brakes ready for later reuse
Friction does work, heating the brakes and slowing the car
The kinetic energy simply disappears when the car stops

questions.explanation: Work done by the friction force between the brakes and the wheel reduces the kinetic energy of the vehicle, and the temperature of the brakes increases.

questions.stem: A car's speed doubles from 10 m/s to 20 m/s. The driver's reaction time and the braking force are unchanged. What happens to the two parts of the stopping distance?

options.text: Both the thinking distance and the braking distance double
Thinking distance doubles and braking distance quadruples
Thinking distance is unchanged, braking distance doubles
The stopping distance itself just doubles overall

questions.explanation: Thinking distance = speed x reaction time, so it doubles. The kinetic energy is four times larger and the same braking force must remove it over a distance, so the braking distance becomes about four times larger.

questions.stem: Five students measure their own reaction times and obtain 0.21 s, 0.34 s, 0.28 s, 0.52 s and 0.45 s. What is the best conclusion to draw?

options.text: Four of the results must be wrong, as only one can be right
Everyone's reaction time is 0.36 s, the mean of the five
The results are unusable because they do not agree
Reaction times differ between people, as expected

questions.explanation: Every value lies inside the typical range of 0.2 s to 0.9 s, and the spread between them is exactly what the specification means by reaction times varying from person to person.

questions.stem: A car is driven on an icy road at the same speed as it was on a dry road. Why is its braking distance longer on the ice?

options.text: The ice makes the vehicle heavier, so it takes far longer
The brakes themselves stop working when the road is icy
There is less grip, so a smaller braking force can act
The driver's reaction time is longer on an icy road

questions.explanation: Ice reduces the friction available where the tyres meet the road, so the largest braking force that can be applied before the wheels lock is smaller and more distance is needed.

questions.stem: Two identical cars must each stop within the same distance, one from 12 m/s and the other from 24 m/s. Which needs the greater braking force, and why?

options.text: The car at 12 m/s, as a slow car is harder to stop
The car at 24 m/s needs less force, having more time
The 24 m/s car needs less force, with more road
The car at 24 m/s: more kinetic energy to remove

questions.explanation: The greater the speed of a vehicle the greater the braking force needed to stop the vehicle in a certain distance. Four times as much kinetic energy must be removed over the same distance.

questions.stem: Two identical lorries brake with the same braking force, one from 15 m/s and one from 25 m/s. Which statement about their stopping distances is correct?

options.text: The 25 m/s lorry needs distance in proportion to speed
The lorry at 15 m/s needs a greater distance in which to stop
The lorry at 25 m/s needs the greater stopping distance
Its braking distance is just under twice as long

questions.explanation: For a given braking force, the greater the speed of the vehicle the greater the stopping distance. The faster lorry travels further while the driver reacts, and further again under braking.

questions.stem: Which list contains only factors that the specification links to a driver's reaction time or ability to react?

options.text: Tiredness, alcohol, drugs, and distractions such as a phone
Tiredness, alcohol, icy roads and worn brake pads
Alcohol, drugs, heavy rain and under-inflated tyres
The driver's age, natural reflexes and their IQ

questions.explanation: The specification names tiredness, drugs and alcohol as affecting reaction time, and adds that distractions may also affect a driver's ability to react.

questions.stem: A car has badly worn tyres. Which part of the stopping distance is increased, and why?

options.text: The thinking distance, because the driver is more cautious
The thinking distance, because tyres are part of the car
Neither, provided the driver brakes gently and early
The braking distance: the tyres grip the road less

questions.explanation: Worn tread cannot clear water or bite into the road surface, so the friction force available for braking is smaller and the car travels further under braking.

questions.stem: A driver brakes very hard to avoid a collision, producing a very large deceleration. Why is this dangerous?

options.text: A very large braking force is needed, risking loss of control
A large deceleration always means a longer stopping distance
It is not dangerous, since stopping sooner is safer
The kinetic energy is destroyed at once, harming the car

questions.explanation: The greater the braking force the greater the deceleration, and large decelerations may lead to the brakes overheating and to loss of control, for example if the wheels lock and the car skids.

questions.stem: (HT only) A car of mass 1200 kg travelling at 24 m/s brakes in an emergency and comes to rest in 3.0 s. Estimate the braking force acting on the car.

options.text: 28 800 N, from the mass times the car's velocity
3600 N, from mass x the 3.0 s stopping time
9600 N, from a = 8.0 m/s2 and then F = m a
150 N, from mass divided by deceleration

questions.explanation: Deceleration a = change in velocity / time = 24 / 3.0 = 8.0 m/s2. Then F = m a = 1200 x 8.0 = 9600 N, a typical order of magnitude for emergency braking of a family car.

questions.stem: (HT only) A van of mass 2000 kg slows from 18 m/s to 6 m/s in 4.0 s while braking on a public road. Estimate the braking force acting on the van.

options.text: 9000 N, taking the change as the full 18 m/s
36 000 N, from mass x the starting speed
500 N, which is a gentle everyday braking force
6000 N, from a deceleration of 3.0 m/s2

questions.explanation: The velocity changes by 12 m/s in 4.0 s, so a = 12 / 4.0 = 3.0 m/s2. Then F = m a = 2000 x 3.0 = 6000 N, a plausible value for firm braking on a public road.
